# Chapter 16 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) He would be grading his own work - the blind spots an audit exists to
find are exactly the ones the builder cannot see, and his incentive is to find
his pipeline sound. Independence beats familiarity: The IT lead or an external
reviewer audits change management; the developer supplies evidence and answers.
(2) Type I says the controls were suitably designed on one day last March - a
snapshot; it says nothing about whether they operated since, and eighteen months
is a long exposure. Ask for the current Type II - design plus operating
effectiveness over the period: The film. (3) ToD: Inspect the backup
configuration and the restore-test procedure - is the control designed to meet
the requirement? Evidence: Configuration export, the documented procedure. ToE:
Sample the year's quarterly restore tests and the nightly job logs - did
backups run and were restores actually performed? Evidence: System-generated job
logs, dated restore-test records. (4) (a) Major - a real, present access risk
(the orphaned accounts of Chapters 8 and 14), exploitable now. (b) Minor - a
document-control weakness (Chapter 15), no direct exposure but a failing
discipline. (c) Major bordering critical - if restores fail, R3's worst case
has no floor; untested recovery is Chapter 12's paper barrier. (5) Action:
Disable the four accounts today; add an HR-to-IT trigger so leaver day means
account-disable day; owner: IT lead; deadline: One week for the accounts, one
month for the trigger; status: Open. Still open next year it becomes a repeat
finding - graded harder because it proves the loop is broken: The organisation
was told, agreed, and did not act, which converts a control gap into a
governance finding.
